summary: HTTP-Enabled Location Delivery (HELD) lets a device ask for its location, and an earlier extension allowed this to be requested using an IP address and port. Some kinds of NAT make that ambiguous unless identifiers for both ends of the packet flow are given. This document defines an XML schema and a URN sub-namespace for a Flow Identity extension to HELD that carries those identifiers.

eli5.summary: Asking "where is this computer?" gets confusing when a middleman hides addresses. This adds extra details about both ends of the conversation so the answer is clear.

questions: locating a device behind nat with held
how to locate a device behind carrier grade nat
what is the held flow element
subtitle: Extra flow details that let a location server find a device hidden behind carrier-grade NAT.

tldr.problem: RFC 6155 let a HELD client ask for its location using an IP address and port number, but some kinds of NAT, notably Carrier Grade NATs, need identifiers for both ends of the packet flow to find the right Device.
tldr.mechanism: A new flow element in the HELD location request names the Layer 3 and Layer 4 protocols and the address and port of the source and destination of the flow, with an optional attribute saying which end is the Target.
tldr.outcome: It gives a general way to identify a Device by a network flow, and the port number elements of RFC 6155 are deprecated and MUST NOT be used in new client implementations.

facts.label: layer4 values
facts.value: udp, tcp, sctp, dccp or a decimal protocol number

today: RFC 6915 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 6155 by deprecating its port number elements. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why a Flow Is Needed
sections.content:
HTTP-Enabled Location Delivery (HELD) lets a client ask a Location Server where a Device is. RFC 6155 added port number identifiers so that HELD requests could work for Devices behind NAT devices. The work was prompted by the Emergency Location Task Group of NICC Standards Limited, the UK telecoms industry standards body.

Later analysis found that with particular types of NAT, and in particular Carrier Grade NATs, the server needs the complete tuple to identify a flow unambiguously: Layer 3 protocol, Layer 4 protocol, source address, source port, destination address and destination port. Only then can it find the true Device.

This document specifies an XML Schema and a URN sub-namespace for a Flow Identity Extension that carries these values.
sections.eli5: Imagine many kids sharing one phone line. To know who is calling, you need to know both who dialed and who was dialed. This extension sends both.

sections.title: The Flow Element
sections.content:
The request carries a <flow> element in the namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:geopriv:held:flow, placed inside an ordinary HELD <locationRequest>. It MUST contain a layer3 attribute with the value ipv4 or ipv6.

It MUST also contain a layer4 attribute. Its value is udp, tcp, sctp or dccp, or a decimal integer for any applicable protocol from the IANA Assigned Internet Protocol Numbers Registry.

Finally it MUST contain a <src> and a <dst> element. Each holds the Layer 3 address and the Layer 4 port number of one end of the flow. The address MUST conform to the IPv4address or IPv6address grammar of RFC 3986.

One attribute is optional: target, with a value of src (the default) or dst. It says which end of the flow is the Target of the location request.
sections.eli5: The request is a little card with both addresses on it and a note saying which one you want to find. If you do not say, it means the sender.

sections.title: The XML Schema
sections.content:
The schema defines a flow element of type flowIdentity. That type is a sequence of one src and one dst, both of type flowEndpoint, plus the attributes target, layer3 and layer4. The layer3 and layer4 attributes are required.

A flowEndpoint contains an address and a port. The port is an unsigned short with a minimum value of 1.
sections.eli5: The schema is the rule book that says what the card must look like, so a computer can check it was filled out correctly.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: The document registers two things under the guidelines of RFC 3688: the XML namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:geopriv:held:flow, and the XML schema from Section 4 under the same URN. The registrant contact for both is the IETF GEOPRIV Working Group.
sections.eli5: The name of the new card type is written in an official list so nobody else uses it by accident.

sections.title: Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
All of the considerations in RFC 6155 apply. Like that RFC, this specification assumes the queried Location Server already has access to the internal state of the network near one end of the flow, for instance the bindings in a NAT on the path.

If that assumption does not hold, the request tells the server about the client's communications that it could not otherwise discern. That may be additional privacy exposure for the client.
sections.eli5: If you hand over details of who you are talking to, the helper learns something about you. Only do it with a helper that could already see the traffic.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document introduces no new security considerations beyond those in RFC 6155.
sections.eli5: Nothing new is risky here beyond what the earlier document already covered.
